title: Learn to Cook: 8 Kitchen Basics Every Beginner Should Know
hook: Cooking feels hard when you're a beginner, but most of it comes down to a handful of habits. Learn these eight kitchen basics, and every recipe you try will turn out better. Chefs use them every day, and you can start with your very next meal. You don't need talent, just practice.
intro: Recipes tell you what to cook, but not how to cook well. The difference between a stressful dinner and a relaxed one usually comes from technique. Prepare before you start, use your knife safely, season as you go, control the heat, and keep your kitchen clean. None of this needs expensive equipment. A sharp knife, a pan, and some attention are enough. Let's go through the eight basics one at a time. Take one basic at a time, and don't try to master everything in a single week.
youNeedNarration: Here's what you need. A sharp chef's knife, which is safer than a dull one. A stable cutting board. A medium skillet. Salt and pepper. A timer, and your phone is fine. And a recipe you'd like to try, since we will use any simple recipe, such as a pasta, an omelet or a stir fry, as our example.
heroImagePrompt: A cook chopping fresh vegetables on a wooden cutting board in a bright home kitchen, pan on the stove behind, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Read the recipe, then prepare
steps.narration: Step one. Before you turn on the heat, read the recipe from start to finish, so there are no surprises. Then do what chefs call mise en place, which means everything in its place. Wash, chop and measure all your ingredients, and set them in small bowls near the stove. Get out the pans and utensils you will need. It feels slow, but it makes cooking calm and fast, because you never have to hunt for an ingredient while something burns. Doing this once will change how you feel about cooking for good.
steps.tip: Prep everything before you heat the pan
steps.imagePrompt: Small glass bowls of chopped vegetables, garlic and spices arranged on a kitchen counter, bright light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Use your knife safely
steps.narration: Step two. Keep your knife sharp, because a dull knife slips and causes cuts. Place a damp cloth under the cutting board so it can't move. Hold the knife with a pinch grip, thumb and forefinger on the blade just above the handle. Curl the fingers of your other hand into a claw shape, with the fingertips tucked back, and rest the flat side of the blade against your knuckles as a guide. Cut slowly, and let the knife do the work. If you're nervous, practise on a carrot or a potato first, slowly, until the movement feels natural.
steps.tip: Fingertips tucked, knuckles guide the blade
steps.imagePrompt: A hand in a claw grip guiding a chef's knife while slicing an onion on a cutting board, close-up, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Season as you go
steps.narration: Step three. Add salt in small amounts at different stages, rather than all at the end. Salt early in cooking helps flavors blend and brings out the taste of vegetables and meat. Taste often, with a clean spoon each time. If a dish is flat, it usually needs salt. If it's too sharp, a little sweetness or fat helps. A squeeze of lemon or a splash of vinegar at the end can brighten a heavy dish. Tasting is the most important skill in cooking. Salt is not the enemy. Under-seasoned food is the most common reason a home-cooked meal tastes bland.
steps.tip: Taste with a clean spoon each time
steps.imagePrompt: A cook tasting sauce from a wooden spoon over a simmering pan on a stove, warm kitchen light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Control the heat
steps.narration: Step four. Most beginners cook on heat that is too high. Preheat your pan for a couple of minutes on medium heat before adding oil, and use high heat only for searing. When food browns too fast or smokes, turn it down. If it's barely sizzling, turn it up. Different pans heat differently, so learn how yours behaves. A good test is to flick a drop of water into the hot pan, which should sizzle immediately. Heat control separates browning from burning. Oil should shimmer, not smoke, before food goes in. If it smokes, remove the pan from the heat for a moment.
steps.tip: Medium heat is your best friend
steps.mistake: Cooking everything on the highest setting
steps.imagePrompt: A frying pan heating on a gas burner with a thin film of oil shimmering, kitchen background, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Don't crowd the pan
steps.narration: Step five. When you put too much food in a pan at once, the temperature drops, and the food steams instead of browning. Mushrooms turn grey, and meat turns pale. Leave a little space between the pieces, and cook in batches if necessary. Keep the first batch warm on a plate. It takes a few extra minutes, but the flavor and texture improve a lot. The same rule applies to roasting vegetables on a tray in the oven. If your recipe feels crowded, a wider pan is a better investment than any gadget.
steps.tip: Space between pieces means a better crust
steps.mistake: Piling everything into one small pan
steps.imagePrompt: Sliced mushrooms browning in a large skillet with space between the pieces, steam rising, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Practice food safety
steps.narration: Step six. Wash your hands with soap before you start, and after handling raw meat, poultry or eggs. Use separate cutting boards, or wash well between uses, so raw juices never touch food that won't be cooked. Keep cold food cold and hot food hot. Cook poultry until it reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, or 74 Celsius, in the thickest part, and use a thermometer to be sure. Put leftovers in the fridge within two hours. Keep raw and cooked foods apart on the table and in the fridge, and store raw meat on the bottom shelf.
steps.mistake: Using one board for raw chicken and salad
steps.imagePrompt: Hands being washed with soap under a running kitchen tap, bright clean kitchen, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Let food rest
steps.narration: Step seven. Many dishes need a pause after cooking. Meat should rest for five to ten minutes so its juices settle, and a cut steak or chicken stays juicy. Roasted vegetables and casseroles are easier to serve after a few minutes. Cooked rice and pasta bake benefit from a short rest too. Use this time to clean your tools, and plate your side dishes. It's the easiest improvement you can make, and it costs nothing. Even a five-minute rest improves most roasted and grilled foods, so plan it into your timing.
steps.tip: Rest meat five to ten minutes
steps.mistake: Cutting meat straight from the heat
steps.imagePrompt: A roast chicken resting on a wooden board covered loosely with foil, warm kitchen light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Clean as you cook
steps.narration: Step eight. Wipe the counter and put things away while the food cooks. Fill the sink with hot soapy water, and wash the tools you have finished with. Keep a bowl on the counter for peels and scraps. A tidy workspace reduces mistakes and stress, and you can enjoy the meal without a mountain of dishes. Always turn pot handles inward, never leave hot pans unattended, and keep a lid nearby to smother any grease fire. Never use water on it. Cleaning as you go also helps you notice what you have left to do, so dinner arrives on time.
steps.tip: Keep a bowl handy for scraps
steps.mistake: Leaving the washing up for later
steps.imagePrompt: A tidy kitchen counter with a bowl of vegetable scraps and a sink with soapy water, photorealistic, no text

mistakesToAvoid.narration: Here are the mistakes to avoid. First, rushing without preparing. Chopping while your onions burn is the fastest road to stress. Second, ignoring the heat. Burnt garlic and raw centers are usually heat problems, not recipe problems. And third, not tasting. A recipe cannot know your ingredients, so your tongue has to be the judge. Follow the recipe, but trust what you taste, and adjust. Everyone burns something at first, and each mistake teaches you something new.
items: Using heat that is too high

recap.narration: Let's recap. Read the recipe and prepare everything first. Use your knife safely. Season as you go. Control the heat. Don't crowd the pan. Practice food safety. Let food rest. And clean as you cook. Eight habits, and every recipe you try will taste better. Cooking is a skill you build with practice, so pick a recipe and start tonight. Practice these eight, and you will cook with confidence.

outro: That's eight kitchen basics every beginner should know. If you feel more confident now, subscribe to WikiTube, because we publish a new how-to every single day. Tell us in the comments what dish you want to learn next. See you tomorrow, and happy cooking.

metadata.title: Learn to Cook: 8 Kitchen Basics Every Beginner Should Know
metadata.description:
New to cooking? In this step-by-step video you'll learn how to cook with eight kitchen basics every beginner should know: reading the recipe and preparing, using a knife safely, seasoning and tasting, controlling the heat, not crowding the pan, food safety, letting food rest, and cleaning as you go. Simple habits that make every recipe better, with no special equipment needed.

You'll need: a sharp chef's knife, a cutting board, a skillet or frying pan, salt and pepper, a kitchen timer or phone.

WikiTube publishes a new step-by-step how-to video every day. Subscribe so you don't miss the next one.
